A cell belongs to the barrio whose outline holds its centre; municipios and Puerto Rico pool the cells of their barrios. 99.5% of the 2,485,382 cells have a value. heat.heat_lst_p90.plain: How hot the hottest tenth of the area's land gets on clear summer mornings: its hot spots, which a median hides.
heat.heat_lst_p90.plain_es: Cuán caliente se pone la décima parte más caliente del terreno del área en mañanas despejadas de verano: sus puntos calientes, que la mediana esconde.
heat.heat_lst_p90.definition: The 90th percentile, over the area's land, of each 60 m cell's land surface temperature on clear summer mornings (the median of the cell's cloud-free Landsat views). In degrees Celsius.
heat.heat_lst_p90.method: heat.py lists every Landsat 8 and 9 Level-2 scene over Puerto Rico of June to September 2024-2026 with less than 70% cloud cover (246 scenes on six path/rows), reads each scene's surface temperature and QA_PIXEL at their first overview (60 m) with raster.py, only the tiles over the barrios, by HTTP range requests, and maps them onto one 60 m grid in UTM zone 20 (scenes in zone 19 through pyproj). An observation counts when QA_PIXEL says clear (bit 6), not cloud shadow, not water and not fill. Each cell's value is the median of its clear views (at least 3; the typical cell has 30). Where USGS has no surface temperature because its emissivity source (ASTER GED) has a gap, the build computes it from the scene's thermal radiance and atmosphere bands with an emissivity read from NDVI, fitted on USGS's own emissivity; against USGS where both exist the method's bias was -0.12, -0.24, +0.20 K on the build's check scenes (13.5% of the cells are mostly filled). A cell belongs to the barrio whose outline holds its centre; municipios and Puerto Rico pool the cells of their barrios. 100.0% of the 2,485,382 cells have a value. Checks at every build: Puerto Rico's median between 25 and 45 °C, San Juan's above it, Jayuya's and Adjuntas's below it.
heat.heat_lst_p90.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: 40.5 °C (its median is 33.4 °C). Highest: Salinas (46.2 °C), Santa Isabel (45.8 °C), Cataño (45.3 °C).
caveats: Surface temperature, not air temperature: roofs, pavement and bare ground get much hotter than the air on a sunny morning, and tree canopy and grass stay closer to it.
Mid-morning (about 10:30 local time) on clear days of the summers: not the afternoon peak, not the night, and not cloudy days.
Elevation cools the land: compare places at similar heights. The Cordillera's barrios are cooler than the coast's for that reason as well as for their tree cover.
Landsat's thermal sensor sees about 100 m; the 60 m cells are finer than what it resolves, so a single roof or park is blurred into its neighbours.

Where USGS's emissivity source has gaps, the build computed the surface temperature itself (same physics, emissivity from vegetation; about half a degree of spread per view against USGS where both exist). Mostly computed this way: Aguada (100%), Aguadilla (100%), Rincón (95%), Moca (83%), Isabela (56%), Maricao (42%), Añasco (40%), Lares (35%), Las Marías (34%), Luquillo (29%), Fajardo (29%), San Sebastián (28%), Camuy (25%), Cayey (23%), Yauco (22%).

heat.heat_res_hot_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 residentes (censo de 2020), cuántos viven aproximadamente en la décima parte más caliente del terreno de Puerto Rico en mañanas despejadas de verano.
heat.heat_res_hot_pct.definition: The share of the area's 2020 census residents whose block's internal point lies on a cell above Puerto Rico's 90th percentile of land surface temperature (40.5 °C). An estimate.
heat.heat_res_hot_pct.method: heat.py lists every Landsat 8 and 9 Level-2 scene over Puerto Rico of June to September 2024-2026 with less than 70% cloud cover (246 scenes on six path/rows), reads each scene's surface temperature and QA_PIXEL at their first overview (60 m) with raster.py, only the tiles over the barrios, by HTTP range requests, and maps them onto one 60 m grid in UTM zone 20 (scenes in zone 19 through pyproj). An observation counts when QA_PIXEL says clear (bit 6), not cloud shadow, not water and not fill. Each cell's value is the median of its clear views (at least 3; the typical cell has 30). Where USGS has no surface temperature because its emissivity source (ASTER GED) has a gap, the build computes it from the scene's thermal radiance and atmosphere bands with an emissivity read from NDVI, fitted on USGS's own emissivity; against USGS where both exist the method's bias was -0.12, -0.24, +0.20 K on the build's check scenes (13.5% of the cells are mostly filled). A cell belongs to the barrio whose outline holds its centre; municipios and Puerto Rico pool the cells of their barrios. 100.0% of the 2,485,382 cells have a value. Checks at every build: Puerto Rico's median between 25 and 45 °C, San Juan's above it, Jayuya's and Adjuntas's below it.
heat.heat_res_hot_pct.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: 37.6% of the residents live on its hottest tenth of land, more than 10% because people live on the warmer lowland and urban land. Highest: Santa Isabel (91.1%), Salinas (80.1%), Ponce (75.7%).

heat.surface_layer.plain: A map layer that colours every 60 m of land by how hot its surface gets on clear summer mornings, or, with the legend's switch, how warm it stays on clear summer nights, from blue (cooler) to red (hotter). In the 3D view it is draped on the terrain under the 3D buildings.
heat.surface_layer.plain_es: Una capa del mapa que colorea cada 60 m de terreno según lo caliente que se pone su superficie en mañanas despejadas de verano o, con el interruptor de la leyenda, lo cálida que se mantiene en noches despejadas de verano, de azul (más fresca) a rojo (más caliente). En la vista 3D se extiende sobre el relieve, debajo de los edificios en 3D.
heat.surface_layer.definition: The median land surface temperature of each 60 m cell (the same values as heat.heat_lst_med, before they are pooled by area), drawn on a diverging scale: grey at Puerto Rico's median, the darkest blue and red at the median minus and plus the larger of the distances from it to the 2nd and 98th percentiles, rounded up to a whole degree; values beyond are drawn at the ends. 64 colour steps. Water and cells with fewer than 3 clear views are transparent. The legend's Morning and Night switch shows the night composite of ecostress.py instead (night_heat_surface.png: ECOSTRESS read at 70 m onto the same grid, its own scale around Puerto Rico's night median); the Colours switch recolours either image for the land in view or for Puerto Rico.
heat.surface_layer.method: heat.py builds the composite (heat.heat_lst_med) and surface_image.py draws it: each pixel of a Web Mercator image of about one cell per pixel takes the value of the cell under its centre (nearest, so nothing is invented between cells), coloured on the scale of heat_surface.json, and written as an indexed PNG with zlib. The 2D map lays it with Leaflet's image overlay, under every other layer; the 3D view adds it as a MapLibre image source, draped on the terrain over the hillshade and under the 3D buildings, at 80% opacity.
heat.surface_layer.how_to_read: Read the colour against Puerto Rico's median: blue land is cooler than the typical surface, red land hotter. It is the surface, not the air, on clear mornings; the mountains are cooler partly because they are higher, so compare places at similar heights. One pixel is one 60 m cell: a cell mixes roofs, streets and trees.
caveats: Landsat's thermal sensor sees about 100 m; the 60 m cells are its pixels resampled, so a street or a single roof is not resolved.
Mid-morning on clear days only (about 10:30): not the afternoon peak, the night or cloudy days.
Land surface temperature, not air temperature: a dark roof can be 20 °C or more above the air.
Night values are ECOSTRESS passes between 21:00 and 06:00, whatever the hour: a place seen mostly before midnight reads a little warmer than one seen mostly before dawn.

Coastal units reach into the sea; the share is measured on the barrio's land as drawn.

layers.reservoirs.plain: Every reservoir with a live USGS gauge on the map: how high its water is now, how it changed in a week, and whether that is usual for this time of year.
layers.reservoirs.plain_es: Cada embalse con un medidor de USGS en vivo en el mapa: qué tan alto está el agua ahora, cuánto cambió en una semana y si eso es usual para esta época del año.
layers.reservoirs.definition: reservoirs.geojson: one point per reservoir with a USGS water-level gauge that reported in the last 30 days and has at least 8 years of daily values in 2011-2025 (25 on 2026-11-02, 19 of them in the Aqueduct and Sewer Authority's daily report). Each point has name, type, municipio, geoid, usgs (the monitoring location), aaa (true for the 19), level and level_time (the latest reading when the file was built), recent_start and recent (120 daily levels in metres, null where missing) and p10, p25, p50, p75, p90 (the usual level for each of the 53 weeks of the year, metres).
layers.reservoirs.method: reservoirs.py reads the USGS Water Data API (no key): the lakes and reservoirs of Puerto Rico, the latest water-surface elevation (parameter 72376, metres above local mean sea level) and the daily values since 2011 (parameter 72375, feet, converted to metres). For each week of the year it takes the mean of that week in each year 2011-2025 and the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th and 90th percentile of those yearly means (at least 8 years). The pop-up says where the latest reading falls: below the 10th percentile is lower than usual for the time of year, above the 90th higher, and between them usual (the level of about 8 years in 10). The chart shades the 10th to 90th percentile and, darker, the 25th to 75th. A finer cut was tried and dropped: where a reservoir is usually kept full, its middle half can be 10 cm wide, so a few centimetres read as 'lower than usual'. On 2026-11-02 the USGS reading matched the level in AAA's 05:00 chart to within 0.08 m for 18 of the 19 reservoirs AAA reports. The 2D map (facilities.js) and the 3D view (facilities3d.js) draw it with core/facilities.js.
layers.reservoirs.how_to_read: Switch the layer on in the Map layers tab of the 2D map or the 3D view (Hazards and environment: Reservoir levels). Click a reservoir for its level now, the change in 7 days, how it compares with the same week in 2011-2025, a chart of the last 120 days over the usual range, and, for the reservoirs in AAA's report, a link to AAA's alert level.
caveats: A level is not a volume: sediment has filled part of several reservoirs, so the same level holds less water than it did when the reservoir was built.

'Usual' means the same week in 2011-2025, a period that includes the droughts of 2015 and 2019-2020 and the years after Hurricane María. An operator can lower a reservoir on purpose, for repairs, dredging or before a storm.
The live reading is provisional, as USGS publishes it; USGS may revise it.
AAA's alert levels (desborde, seguridad, observación, ajustes, control) are not published here: AAA states no licence for them. The pop-up links to AAA's own page.
When the layer is switched on, the visitor's browser asks USGS's server for the latest readings, as the sea level rise layer asks NOAA's for its tiles.

layers.groundwater.plain: Every well with a live USGS gauge on the map: how far below the ground the water stands now, how that changed in a week, and whether it is usual for this time of year.
layers.groundwater.plain_es: Cada pozo con un medidor de USGS en vivo en el mapa: a qué profundidad bajo el terreno está el agua ahora, cuánto cambió en una semana y si eso es usual para esta época del año.
layers.groundwater.definition: groundwater.geojson: one point per well of the US Geological Survey that reported a depth to water in the last 30 days (34 wells in 24 municipios on 2026-11-12). Depth to water is how far below the ground the water stands in the well, here in metres: a larger number is lower water. Each point has name, type, municipio, geoid, usgs (the monitoring location), station (the name USGS gives the well), depth and depth_time (the latest reading when the file was built), well_depth (how deep the well was built, where USGS records it), recent_start and recent (120 daily depths, null where missing) and p10, p25, p50, p75, p90 (the usual depth for each of the 53 weeks of the year; null where the well has fewer than 8 years of daily values).
layers.groundwater.method: groundwater.py reads the USGS Water Data API (no key): the wells of Puerto Rico, the latest depth to water (parameter 72019, feet below land surface) and the daily values since 2011, converted to metres (x 0.3048). USGS keeps one daily statistic per well, the mean of the day or the reading at noon; the build takes the mean where the well has it. For each week of the year it takes the mean of that week in each year 2011-2025 and the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th and 90th percentile of those yearly means (at least 8 years), the method of the Reservoir levels layer. The pop-up says where the latest reading falls: deeper than the 90th percentile is water lower than usual for the time of year, shallower than the 10th is water higher than usual, and between them usual (the depth of about 8 years in 10). The chart draws the last 120 days over the shaded 10th to 90th percentile, with the ground towards the top.
layers.groundwater.how_to_read: Switch the layer on in the Map layers tab of the 2D map or the 3D view (Environment and climate: Groundwater levels). Click a well for the depth to water now, the change in seven days, how it compares with the same week in 2011-2025, a chart of the last 120 days over the usual range, the depth of the well and a link to the well's page at USGS.
caveats: A well shows the water at one point of one aquifer. Pumping from that well or one nearby can lower the water within hours, so a single low reading is not a drought, and the next well can read differently.
The layer says nothing about the quality of the water (salt, nitrate or other contamination) or about how much water can be pumped.
The live reading is provisional, as USGS publishes it; USGS may revise it.

'Usual' means the same week in 2011-2025, a period that includes the droughts of 2015 and 2019-2020 and Hurricanes Irma, María and Fiona. 5 of the 34 wells have fewer than 8 years of daily values and show no usual range.

Only wells that report now are drawn: 34 of the 5,197 well sites USGS lists for Puerto Rico, most of which were measured a few times or stopped reporting years ago. Large parts of the island have no well in the layer.
The wells are named as USGS names them, often with the code of the well field (JUA 5, MW 11).
When the layer is switched on, the visitor's browser asks USGS's server for the latest readings, as the Reservoir levels layer does.

layers.rain.plain: Every USGS rain gauge that is reporting now on the map: how much rain fell in the last 24 hours and the last 7 days, and whether that week is usual for this time of year.
layers.rain.plain_es: Cada pluviómetro de USGS que está informando ahora en el mapa: cuánta lluvia cayó en las últimas 24 horas y en los últimos 7 días, y si esa semana es usual para esta época del año.
layers.rain.definition: rain_gauges.geojson: one point per site of the US Geological Survey that reported precipitation in the last 30 days (54 gauges in 30 municipios on 2026-11-12; 20 are rain gauges of their own and the others are the rain gauge of a river, reservoir or well station). Rain is given in millimetres (25.4 mm is one inch). Each point has name, type, municipio, geoid, usgs (the monitoring location), station (the name USGS gives the site), recent_start and recent (120 daily totals, null where missing) and p10, p25, p50, p75, p90 (the usual rain of a week for each of the 53 weeks of the year; null where the gauge has fewer than 8 years of daily totals).
layers.rain.method: rain_gauges.py reads the USGS Water Data API (no key): every site inside Puerto Rico's box with a precipitation reading (parameter 00045, inches), its name, and its daily totals since 2011 (statistic 00006, the sum of the day), converted to millimetres (x 25.4). For each week of the year it takes the rain of that week in each year 2011-2025 (the mean of its daily totals times seven; a week needs six of its days) and the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th and 90th percentile of those yearly weeks (at least 8 years). When the layer is switched on, the page asks USGS for the 15-minute readings of the last 24 hours, which it adds up, and for the daily totals of the last 8 days. The pop-up gives the 24-hour total, the total of the last 7 whole days, and where that falls: below the 10th percentile is drier than usual for the time of year, above the 90th wetter, and between them usual. The chart draws one bar for each of the 120 days before the file was built.
layers.rain.how_to_read: Switch the layer on in the Map layers tab of the 2D map or the 3D view (Environment and climate: Rainfall). Click a gauge for the rain of the last 24 hours, the rain of the last 7 days, how that compares with the same time of year in 2011-2025, a bar for each of the last 120 days and a link to the gauge's page at USGS. Turn on River flow to see how the rivers answered.
caveats: A gauge measures the rain at one spot. A shower a kilometre wide can miss it, so the rain over a barrio or a watershed can be very different from the gauge's.
This is not a flood warning or a forecast. The National Weather Service issues warnings and forecasts, and maps rain between the gauges with radar.
The readings are provisional, as USGS publishes them. A gauge can clog, be damaged or stop reporting during a storm, which reads as less rain than fell.

The 7-day total is compared with calendar weeks of 2011-2025; in the dry season the usual range of some gauges starts at or near zero, so a week without rain reads as usual. 9 of the 54 gauges have fewer than 8 years of daily totals and show no usual range.

The gauges are not spread evenly: most stand at river and reservoir stations or in the Río Grande de Loíza basin above Caguas, and 48 municipios have none. The National Weather Service's own gauges are not in this layer.
When the layer is switched on, the visitor's browser asks USGS's server for the latest readings, as the Reservoir levels layer does.
layers.rain.source_detail: USGS Water Data API (api.waterdata.usgs.gov/ogcapi/v1): latest-continuous (00045, by bounding box), monitoring-locations (names), daily (00045, statistic 00006) and, from the page, continuous (00045, the last 24 hours)

layers.rivers.plain: Every river and stream with a live USGS gauge on the map: how much water is passing now, how that compares with a week ago, and whether it is usual for this time of year.
layers.rivers.plain_es: Cada río y quebrada con un medidor de USGS en vivo en el mapa: cuánta agua pasa ahora, cómo se compara con hace una semana y si eso es usual para esta época del año.
layers.rivers.definition: river_gauges.geojson: one point per stream gauge of the US Geological Survey that reported a discharge in the last 30 days and has at least 8 years of daily values in 2011-2025 (71 gauges on 54 rivers and streams on 2026-11-11). Discharge is the volume of water that passes the gauge each second, here in cubic metres per second (m³/s). Each point has name (the river or stream), type, municipio, geoid, usgs (the monitoring location), station (the name USGS gives the gauge), flow and flow_time (the latest reading when the file was built), recent_start and recent (120 daily mean flows, null where missing) and p10, p25, p50, p75, p90 (the usual flow for each of the 53 weeks of the year). Since 2026-11-12 each gauge also carries its gauge height (how high the water stands on the gauge's own scale, in metres), and, where USGS has surveyed them, flood reference levels: the top of the riverbank, the lowest beam and the deck of a bridge, a past flood's high-water mark (1 gauge on 2026-11-12: Río de la Plata at Comerío).
layers.rivers.method: river_gauges.py reads the USGS Water Data API (no key): the stream sites of Puerto Rico, the latest discharge (parameter 00060, cubic feet per second) and the daily mean discharge since 2011 (statistic 00003), both converted to cubic metres per second (x 0.0283168). For each week of the year it takes the mean of that week in each year 2011-2025 and the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th and 90th percentile of those yearly means (at least 8 years), the method of the Reservoir levels layer. The pop-up says where the latest reading falls: below the 10th percentile is lower than usual for the time of year, above the 90th higher, and between them usual (the flow of about 8 years in 10). The latest reading is one moment and the usual range is made of weekly means, so a short burst of rain can read as higher than usual. The chart draws the last 120 days over the shaded 10th to 90th percentile (darker: 25th to 75th) on a logarithmic scale, because a storm's flow can be hundreds of times a dry week's. The river's name is the start of the USGS station name, with its accents restored; the pop-up gives the station name as USGS writes it and links to the gauge's USGS page. The 2D map (facilities.js) and the 3D view (facilities3d.js) draw it with core/facilities.js. The gauge height (parameter 00065, feet, kept in metres) is the latest reading of each gauge. The flood reference levels come from USGS Real-Time Flood Impacts; each is a gauge height, so the pop-up can say how far the water is from it. A gauge height is measured from the gauge's own zero, not from sea level, so two gauges cannot be compared. The flood stages come from the National Weather Service's National Water Prediction Service: each NWS gauge names its USGS site, and its stages are gauge heights in feet on that site's scale, converted to metres. A gauge keeps them only where they are in feet, rise from action to major and, when both agencies' latest readings were taken within an hour, the two agree to half a foot.
layers.rivers.how_to_read: Switch the layer on in the Map layers tab of the 2D map or the 3D view (Environment and climate: River flow). Click a gauge for the flow now, the flow seven days ago, how it compares with the same week in 2011-2025, a chart of the last 120 days over the usual range, and a link to the gauge's page at USGS. Turn on Flood zones or Watersheds and streams to see what lies downstream. For most gauges the pop-up also gives the National Weather Service's flood stages (action, minor, moderate, major), which one the water has reached, and how far it is from each.
caveats: Nothing in this layer is a flood warning. A flow higher than usual is not one, and neither is water above a flood stage: the National Weather Service issues the warnings. The stages are those NWS has set for 66 of the 71 gauges, read once a month, so one NWS revised since may be out of date here; the pop-up links to the gauge's NWS page. A river can also leave its banks between two gauges.
The live reading is provisional, as USGS publishes it; USGS may revise it. During a flood a gauge can be damaged or stop reporting, and the pop-up then shows the last reading it has, with its time.
Some gauges are below a dam, a water intake or an irrigation canal: their flow is what the operator lets through, not what the rain brings.
'Usual' means the same week in 2011-2025, a period that includes the droughts of 2015 and 2019-2020 and Hurricanes Irma, María and Fiona.

Only gauges that report now and have 8 years of record are drawn: 71 of the 1,083 stream sites USGS lists for Puerto Rico, most of which stopped reporting years ago or were measured only a few times. Many rivers and most streams have no gauge.
A flow is not a water level: the same flow is deep in a narrow channel and shallow in a wide one.
When the layer is switched on, the visitor's browser asks USGS's server for the latest readings, as the Reservoir levels layer does.

The flood reference levels are surveyed points at one place on the river. Water below them there does not mean no flooding elsewhere, and they do not replace a warning from the National Weather Service.
layers.rivers.source_detail: USGS Water Data API (api.waterdata.usgs.gov/ogcapi/v1): monitoring-locations (site_type_code ST, state 72), latest-continuous (00060) and daily (00060, statistic 00003); latest-continuous (00065, gauge height; 00010, water temperature, which no river gauge reported on 2026-11-12); USGS Real-Time Flood Impacts (api.waterdata.usgs.gov/rtfi-api), reference points of Puerto Rico; NWS National Water Prediction Service API (api.water.noaa.gov/nwps/v1/gauges): flood categories

water.watersheds_layer.plain: The subwatersheds of Puerto Rico, the areas whose rain drains to one stretch of river, with the main streams.
water.watersheds_layer.plain_es: Las subcuencas de Puerto Rico, las áreas cuya lluvia drena a un tramo de río, con las quebradas y ríos principales.
water.watersheds_layer.definition: watersheds.geojson holds the 227 subwatersheds (HUC-12) of the USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset in Puerto Rico, drawn as dashed outlines, with their subbasin (HUC-8), area and 2020 residents; streams.geojson holds the 3,992 flowlines of NHDPlus High Resolution that drain 5 km² or more, drawn wider for larger rivers. A click on the map names the subwatershed there.
water.watersheds_layer.method: watersheds.py reads both from The National Map's ArcGIS services (subregion and VPU 2101), simplified to about 20 m. Residents are the 2020 census blocks whose point is inside each subwatershed, as the study areas count them; they add up to 3,285,324 of Puerto Rico's 3,285,874.
water.watersheds_layer.how_to_read: Each dashed outline is the land that drains to one stretch of river. The blue lines are the streams, wider for larger rivers. For the land that drains to any point, use What drains here in Tools › Analysis › Study areas.
caveats: Outlines and lines are simplified to about 20 m.
Small streams (draining less than 5 km²) are not drawn, though What drains here uses them.

water.watersheds_layer.source_detail: USGS WBD (wbd/MapServer layers 6 and 4) and NHDPlus HR (NHDPlus_HR/MapServer layer 3), read 2026-11-10.

water.what_drains_here.plain: A tool that traces the land whose rain flows to a point you pick, down the USGS stream network, and summarises it like any study area.
water.what_drains_here.plain_es: Una herramienta que traza el terreno cuya lluvia corre hasta un punto que usted escoge, por la red de quebradas del USGS, y lo resume como cualquier área de estudio.
water.what_drains_here.definition: catchments.geojson holds the 13,809 catchments of NHDPlus High Resolution in Puerto Rico (8,860.4 km2), each linked to the next one downstream by its stream's hydrologic sequence, and each minor branch linked to the reaches it splits from. Picking a point finds the catchment under it and walks the links upstream in the browser; the catchments found become one study area.
water.what_drains_here.method: Checks at every build: 12,000 to 16,000 catchments and flowlines, the links valid and without a cycle, the catchments adding up to 8,500 to 10,500 km2, 200 to 260 subwatersheds, 99% of the residents in one, and the drainage area of the five largest rivers and of the largest minor branch within 3% of NHDPlus's own: Río Grande De Loiza 750 km2 (NHDPlus 750); Río Grande de Arecibo 655 km2 (NHDPlus 655); Río Grande de Manati 593 km2 (NHDPlus 593); Río Cocal 586 km2 (NHDPlus 586); Río de la Plata 568 km2 (NHDPlus 568); (no name) (minor branch) 544 km2 (NHDPlus 544).
water.what_drains_here.how_to_read: The area found is the land that drains to the stream next to the point, from the whole catchment the point is in. A point on a hillside gets its catchment and everything upstream of it.
caveats: Water is routed down each river's main path, as NHDPlus does; canals and pipes that move water between basins are not followed.
Outlines are simplified to about 20 m, so the edge of the area is approximate.
water.what_drains_here.geography: Puerto Rico, Vieques, Culebra and Mona
water.what_drains_here.source_detail: USGS NHDPlus HR (NHDPlus_HR/MapServer layers 3 and 10), VPU 2101, read 2026-11-10.

slope.slope_steep15_pct.plain: Out of every 100 parts of the area's land, how many are steeper than 15%: where building and farming begin to need terraces or special design.
slope.slope_steep15_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 partes del terreno del área, cuántas tienen más de 15 % de pendiente: donde construir y cultivar empieza a requerir terrazas o un diseño especial.
slope.slope_steep15_pct.definition: The share of the area's 10 m cells whose slope is more than 15%, by Horn's method on the USGS 3DEP 1/3 arc-second elevation model.
slope.slope_steep15_pct.method: slope.py reads the USGS 3DEP 1/3 arc-second elevation tiles over Puerto Rico in windows of 0.1 degree (raster.py) and computes the slope of every 10 m cell by Horn's method, with the cell's size in metres at its latitude, as rise over run x 100; a cell next to one with no height has no slope. The cells are counted in blocks of 6 x 6 (about 60 m); a block belongs to the barrio that holds its centre (the nearest within 100 m off the coast), and blocks in no barrio (the sea) are left out. Municipios and Puerto Rico pool their barrios' cells. Checks at every build: Puerto Rico's share steeper than 30% between 15% and 55%; Jayuya, Orocovis and Barranquitas steeper than Puerto Rico; Cataño with less than 5% of its land steeper than 15%; the cells counted cover 97% to 110% of the barrios' Census land area.
slope.slope_steep15_pct.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: 61.7%. Highest: Maricao (95.4%), Orocovis (93.7%), Adjuntas (92.7%). Lowest: Loíza (1.2%), Cataño (2.0%).
caveats: Heights are of the bare ground at about 10 m: cuts, retaining walls and terraces narrower than a cell are smoothed out, and a road on a bridge reads the ground below.
A block of about 60 m across a barrio's edge counts whole in the barrio that holds its centre.
Inland water (lagoons, reservoirs) inside a barrio's outline counts as flat land.
The thresholds are planning guides, not rules for a site: whether a parcel can be built on depends on its soil, geology and drainage, and on the regulations.
slope.slope_steep15_pct.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios

vegetation.veg_dense_pct.plain: How much of the area's land is densely vegetated on clear summer days, such as forest or crops in full leaf.
vegetation.veg_dense_pct.plain_es: Qué parte del terreno del área tiene vegetación densa en días despejados de verano, como bosque o cultivos con todas sus hojas.
vegetation.veg_dense_pct.definition: The share of the area's land cells whose NDVI is 0.6 or more, over its cells with a value. USGS gives about 0.6 to 0.9 for dense vegetation such as forests and crops at their peak.
vegetation.veg_dense_pct.method: vegetation.py lists every Sentinel-2 Level-2A scene over Puerto Rico of June to September 2024-2026 with less than 70% cloud cover (984 scenes on eight MGRS tiles, 241 passes), reads each scene's red and near-infrared bands and its scene classification at 40 m with raster.py, only the tiles over the barrios, by HTTP range requests, and maps them onto heat.py's 60 m grid in UTM zone 20 (scenes in zone 19 through pyproj). An observation counts when the scene classification says vegetation or not vegetated (clouds, cirrus, shadows, water and unclassified pixels are left out); where two tiles of one pass overlap, a cell keeps one view. NDVI = (near-infrared − red) / (near-infrared + red). Each cell's value is the median of its clear views (at least 3; the typical cell has 30). A cell belongs to the barrio whose outline holds its centre; municipios and Puerto Rico pool the cells of their barrios. 99.4% of the 2,485,382 cells have a value. Checks at every build: Puerto Rico's median NDVI between 0.4 and 0.9, San Juan's below it, Jayuya's and Adjuntas's above it, and greener barrios cooler in the surface heat file (a Spearman rank correlation of −0.3 or less; -0.894 across 901 barrios in this build).
vegetation.veg_dense_pct.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: 75.7%. Highest: Maricao (97.4%), Las Marías (97.1%), Utuado (95.7%). Lowest: Santa Isabel (16.6%), Lajas (22.9%), Guánica (27.4%).
caveats: NDVI shows how green the land looks from above, not tree cover: a lawn or a pasture in leaf can read as green as a forest, and a tree's shade on a street is not counted as such.
Summer (June to September) on clear days: dry-season vegetation, after a drought or after a hurricane, reads lower.
Read at 40 m: each pixel mixes roofs, yards, streets and trees, so a city street lined with trees reads in between, and a single park smaller than a pixel is blurred into its neighbours.

vegetation.veg_ndvi_med.plain: How green the area's land typically looks from a satellite on clear summer days, from 0 (pavement, roofs, bare ground) to about 0.9 (dense forest): half its land is greener than this.
vegetation.veg_ndvi_med.plain_es: Cuán verde se ve por lo general el terreno del área desde un satélite en días despejados de verano, de 0 (pavimento, techos, suelo desnudo) a cerca de 0.9 (bosque denso): la mitad de su terreno es más verde que esto.
vegetation.veg_ndvi_med.definition: The median, over the area's land, of each 60 m cell's NDVI on clear summer days (the median of the cell's cloud-free Sentinel-2 views). NDVI = (near-infrared − red) / (near-infrared + red).
vegetation.veg_ndvi_med.method: vegetation.py lists every Sentinel-2 Level-2A scene over Puerto Rico of June to September 2024-2026 with less than 70% cloud cover (984 scenes on eight MGRS tiles, 241 passes), reads each scene's red and near-infrared bands and its scene classification at 40 m with raster.py, only the tiles over the barrios, by HTTP range requests, and maps them onto heat.py's 60 m grid in UTM zone 20 (scenes in zone 19 through pyproj). An observation counts when the scene classification says vegetation or not vegetated (clouds, cirrus, shadows, water and unclassified pixels are left out); where two tiles of one pass overlap, a cell keeps one view. NDVI = (near-infrared − red) / (near-infrared + red). Each cell's value is the median of its clear views (at least 3; the typical cell has 30). A cell belongs to the barrio whose outline holds its centre; municipios and Puerto Rico pool the cells of their barrios. 99.4% of the 2,485,382 cells have a value. Checks at every build: Puerto Rico's median NDVI between 0.4 and 0.9, San Juan's below it, Jayuya's and Adjuntas's above it, and greener barrios cooler in the surface heat file (a Spearman rank correlation of −0.3 or less; -0.894 across 901 barrios in this build).
vegetation.veg_ndvi_med.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: 0.78. Greenest municipios: Las Marías (0.87), Utuado (0.85), Maricao (0.85). Least green: San Juan (0.31), Cataño (0.37), Santa Isabel (0.41).
caveats: NDVI shows how green the land looks from above, not tree cover: a lawn or a pasture in leaf can read as green as a forest, and a tree's shade on a street is not counted as such.
Summer (June to September) on clear days: dry-season vegetation, after a drought or after a hurricane, reads lower.
Read at 40 m: each pixel mixes roofs, yards, streets and trees, so a city street lined with trees reads in between, and a single park smaller than a pixel is blurred into its neighbours.

exposure.hu_protected.plain: How many housing units are inside the outline of a protected area such as a park, forest or reserve, counted for each municipio, barrio and census tract.
exposure.hu_protected.plain_es: Cuántas unidades de vivienda hay dentro del contorno de un área protegida, como un parque, un bosque o una reserva, en cada municipio, barrio y sector censal.
exposure.hu_protected.definition: Two fields hold the count for each area. protected: the housing units of every census block whose internal point lies inside a USGS PAD-US protected area, other than a proclamation boundary (which outlines whole islands or refuges and is not managed land). protected_strict: the same inside areas with GAP status 1 or 2 (a strict nature reserve, or land managed for biodiversity). Both read site/data/protected.geojson. For the whole island, 30,778 housing units (1.9%) are inside a protected area and 16,046 (1.0%) inside a strictly protected one.
exposure.hu_protected.method: exposure.py counts each 2020 Census block whole, by its internal point (the Census Bureau's point that always lies inside the block): inside the polygons of a layer, or within 400 m of a stop. It adds the block's 2020 housing units up to the municipio, the barrio and the census tract that hold it, so the three files agree and counts add up exactly between levels. It writes nothing unless every area's total equals the crosswalk's and every set lies inside its superset (the area flooded at 2 ft is inside the area flooded at 3 ft; a stop with a current timetable is a stop).
exposure.hu_protected.how_to_read: Compare areas by share: divide a count by the area's total (the total field), which puts a small barrio and a large municipio on one scale. To get a share for a group of areas (the island, a region), add the counts and the totals first, then divide; do not average the shares. It shows where homes lie within the outline of conserved land, which matters for planning, not how many people live on managed public land.
caveats: PAD-US includes parks, forests, refuges, local recreation areas and conservation lands, so an urban park counts. An outline can also include private land inside the boundary of a reserve.
A census block is counted whole by one point, so a block that a boundary cuts is counted in or out by its internal point: near an edge the count can be higher or lower than the true number.
A housing unit is a house, an apartment, a mobile home or a room meant as separate living quarters; people in group quarters (a dormitory, a nursing home) are not in housing units.
exposure.hu_protected.geography: 78 municipios, 901 barrios and 981 census tracts, in three files
exposure.hu_protected.source_detail: 2020 Census blocks (TIGERweb layer 10); USGS PAD-US 4.1, as published in protected.geojson

municipalities.landuse_km2.plain: How many square kilometres of the municipality the 2015 land use plan puts in each of four groups: urban, urbanizable, ordinary rural and especially protected rural. Water and roads are left out.
municipalities.landuse_km2.plain_es: Cuántos kilómetros cuadrados del municipio coloca el Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015 en cada uno de cuatro grupos: urbano, urbanizable, rústico común y rústico especialmente protegido. El agua y las vías quedan fuera.
municipalities.landuse_km2.definition: An object with up to four numbers, in square kilometres rounded to one decimal: urban, urbanizable, rustic (ordinary rural) and protected. Each is the summed area of the plan polygons of that group that the plan assigns to the municipality. A group is missing when the municipality has no polygon of that class. A value of 0.0 means a polygon exists but its area rounds to 0.0 km² (under 0.05 km²). Class codes: see municipalities.landuse_classes.
municipalities.landuse_km2.method: landuse.py reads the Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015 polygons, maps each class to a group, and sums each polygon's Shape_Area (square metres in the plan's projected coordinates) divided by 1,000,000 per municipality and group, using the municipality named in the plan. Water and road polygons are not summed. See land.put_statistics.
municipalities.landuse_km2.how_to_read: Use the areas when you need square kilometres. For shares, use urban_pct, urbanizable_pct, rustic_common_pct and protected_land_pct. In the CSV (comma-separated values, spreadsheet) download the object becomes four columns: landuse_km2_urban, landuse_km2_urbanizable, landuse_km2_rustic and landuse_km2_protected. A column is blank where the municipality has no polygon of that group. In the 2015 plan, urbanizable land is missing for 27 municipalities and ordinary rural land for Cataño, and the four values add to 8,409.1 km² for the island, about 95% of the Census land area (8,868.5 km²).
caveats: A plan designation from 2015: it shows how the Junta de Planificación classified the land, not today's land cover or what stands on it.

The classified area can be well under the Census land area. In the 2015 plan, Mayagüez covers 134.0 of 200.9 km²: the plan has no polygon on Isla de Mona, which the Census boundary places in Mayagüez, so Mayagüez's figures leave Mona out.
Polygons are assigned by the municipality name in the plan, not by cutting them at the Census boundary.
The Plan's own version fields read PUT-2014 and 30-NOV-2015; this dictionary calls the version dated 30 November 2015 PUT 2015 (see land.put_layer).

The Junta de Planificación states no data license, and its site footer reads "Todos los derechos reservados". Check its terms before reusing the plan or figures computed from it. The Junta's page (read 2026-10-03) gives the plan a ten-year term and lists a review process for a new plan (PUT-2025). These figures describe the 2015 plan only.

values.urbanizable: Land classed Suelo Urbanizable Programado (SURP) or Suelo Urbanizable No Programado (SURNP).
values.rustic: Land classed Suelo Rústico Común (SRC), ordinary rural land.
values.protected: Land classed Suelo Rústico Especialmente Protegido (SREP and its subtypes).

municipalities.rustic_common_pct.plain: Out of every 100 square kilometres of classified land in the municipality, how many the 2015 land use plan marks as ordinary rural land (Suelo Rústico Común). Water and roads are left out.
municipalities.rustic_common_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 kilómetros cuadrados de terreno clasificado en el municipio, cuántos marca el Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015 como suelo rústico común (Suelo Rústico Común). El agua y las vías quedan fuera.
municipalities.rustic_common_pct.definition: Area of plan polygons of class SRC (Suelo Rústico Común, ordinary rural land) divided by the area of all urban, urbanizable, ordinary rural and protected polygons of the municipality, times 100.
municipalities.rustic_common_pct.method: Summed area of the plan polygons of the group, assigned to the municipality by the plan's municipality name, divided by the summed area of the four groups (urban, urbanizable, ordinary rural, protected), times 100, rounded to one decimal. Water and road polygons are in neither the numerator nor the denominator. See land.put_statistics.
municipalities.rustic_common_pct.how_to_read: Ordinary rural land is the plan's rural class without the special-protection label. A high value means much of the municipality is rural land the plan does not single out for protection. In the 2015 plan the share ranges from 0.0% (Cataño) to 65.0% (Rincón). No map or page shows this field; it is in municipalities.json and in the CSV (comma-separated values) download.
caveats: A plan designation from 2015: it shows how the Junta de Planificación classified the land, not today's land cover or what stands on it.

Shares are of classified land only. Water and road polygons are left out, so in the 2015 plan the classified area is 67% (Mayagüez) to 98% (Villalba) of the Census land area. Mayagüez covers 134.0 of 200.9 km²: the plan has no polygon on Isla de Mona, which the Census boundary places in Mayagüez, so its shares leave Mona out. The four shares are rounded to one decimal, so they can add to 99.9 or 100.1.
Rural land with special protection is a separate group (protected_land_pct).

municipalities.protected_land_pct.plain: Out of every 100 square kilometres of classified land in the municipality, how many the 2015 land use plan marks as specially protected rural land. Water and roads are left out.
municipalities.protected_land_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 kilómetros cuadrados de terreno clasificado en el municipio, cuántos marca el Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015 como suelo rústico especialmente protegido. El agua y las vías quedan fuera.
municipalities.protected_land_pct.definition: Area of plan polygons of class SREP (Suelo Rústico Especialmente Protegido) and its subtypes (SREP-A, SREP-E, SREP-H, SREP-AE, SREP-AH, SREP-AP, SREP-EA, SREP-EH, SREP-EP, SREP-P) divided by the area of all urban, urbanizable, ordinary rural and protected polygons of the municipality, times 100.
municipalities.protected_land_pct.method: Summed area of the plan polygons of the group, assigned to the municipality by the plan's municipality name, divided by the summed area of the four groups (urban, urbanizable, ordinary rural, protected), times 100, rounded to one decimal. Water and road polygons are in neither the numerator nor the denominator. See land.put_statistics.
municipalities.protected_land_pct.how_to_read: A high value means the plan designates most of the municipality's land for special protection (agricultural, ecological, water-related or landscape value). In the 2015 plan the share ranges from 0.1% (Cataño) to 96.7% (Maricao); island-wide it is 63.8% (5,361.0 of 8,409.1 km² of classified land). The value does not say what may be built on any parcel; it measures plan area only. Ask the Junta de Planificación or the municipality about any decision on a parcel.

environment.landuse_class_areas.plain: How many square kilometres of each municipality, and of all of Puerto Rico, the 2015 land use plan puts in each of its classes: urban, land for planned or reserve growth, ordinary rural, and the kinds of specially protected rural land. It is the data behind the land-use analysis.
environment.landuse_class_areas.plain_es: Cuántos kilómetros cuadrados de cada municipio, y de todo Puerto Rico, pone el plan de uso de terrenos de 2015 en cada una de sus clases: urbano, suelo para crecimiento programado o de reserva, rústico común y los tipos de rústico especialmente protegido. Son los datos del análisis de uso de terrenos.
environment.landuse_class_areas.definition: landuse_summary.json holds one field per class (SU, SURP, SURNP, SRC, SREP, SREP-E, SREP-A, SREP-H, SREP-EH, SREP-AH, AGUA, VIAL): the km² of that class in each municipio (municipios, keyed by name, listed in names), in Puerto Rico (puerto_rico, the sum of the municipios) and in polygons with no municipio (unassigned). classes gives each class its label, group (urban, urbanizable, rustic, protected, water, road), colour (the map's) and in_share: false for water (AGUA) and road rights-of-way (VIAL), which shares of land leave out. SREP covers the specially protected rural land with no sub-class of its own colour (codes such as SREP-AE, SREP-EP, SREP-EA, SREP-P, SREP-AP), as the map draws it.
environment.landuse_class_areas.method: landuse.py (class_summary) adds the Shape_Area of the full-resolution polygons (square metres in the projected CRS, divided by 1,000,000), by class and by municipio, before the display copy is simplified. Rounded to 0.001 km². The four groups add up to the landuse_km2 of municipalities.json, which the urban_pct, protected_land_pct and the other share fields divide by.
environment.landuse_class_areas.how_to_read: Divide a class by the land in the plan (all classes with in_share) for a share; the analysis does it for you. In the 2026-10 snapshot Puerto Rico has 8,409.1 km² of land in the plan: 14.2% urban, 0.8% for urban growth, 21.3% ordinary rural and 63.7% specially protected rural, most of it agricultural (27.7%) or ecological (21.3%). Cataño is 99.9% urban and San Juan 79.6%; Maricao is 96.7% specially protected and Las Marías 94.3%.

municipalities.landuse_share_method.plain: Land shares divide plan area by plan area. Place shares divide listings by listings. Water and roads are left out of the land shares but stay in the denominator of the place shares. This entry gives the steps.
municipalities.landuse_share_method.plain_es: Las proporciones de terreno dividen área del plan entre área del plan. Las proporciones de lugares dividen registros entre registros. El agua y las vías quedan fuera de las proporciones de terreno, pero se mantienen en el denominador de las proporciones de lugares. Esta entrada da los pasos.
municipalities.landuse_share_method.definition: Area shares (urban_pct, urbanizable_pct, rustic_common_pct, protected_land_pct and landuse_km2): for each municipality the build sums the area of its plan polygons by group and leaves out water and road. Each share is the group's area divided by the summed area of the four groups, times 100, rounded to one decimal. Place shares (places_on_protected_land, places_on_protected_land_pct, places_urban_pct): each listing is tested against the plan polygons; the share is the listings in the group divided by the listings inside any polygon, including water and road.
municipalities.landuse_share_method.method: landuse.py reads the plan polygons from the Junta de Planificación's official shapefile (reprojected to WGS84) or from the plan's hosted ArcGIS Online copy. Area is the plan's Shape_Area (square metres in the plan's projected coordinates) divided by 1,000,000. A polygon belongs to the municipality named in its Municipio attribute, matched to the 78 names ignoring accents and capitals. A listing belongs to the first polygon that contains its point. The statistics use the full polygons; landuse.geojson is a simplified display copy.
municipalities.landuse_share_method.how_to_read: Use area shares to describe the land and place shares to describe where listed places stand. The two can differ a lot: land that is mostly protected can hold few listings. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 32,369 of the island's 32,541 listings fall inside a plan polygon.
caveats: The area is the plan's polygon area, not the Census land area, so in the 2015 plan a municipality's classified area can be well under its land area (Mayagüez 67%, because the plan has no polygon on Isla de Mona).
A plan polygon whose municipality name matches none of the 78 names is skipped. The plan has one such polygon, a water polygon named Guayanabo, so it changes no share.
The observatory does not include the Calificación (zoning districts) layer of the Junta de Planificación, which was not available when the 2026-10 snapshot was built.

municipalities.landuse_classes.plain: The 2015 land use plan labels each piece of land with a class code. The observatory gathers the codes into six groups: urban, urbanizable, ordinary rural, protected, water and road. The land-area shares use the first four groups; the place shares keep water and road polygons in the denominator.
municipalities.landuse_classes.plain_es: El Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015 identifica cada porción de terreno con un código de clase. El observatorio reúne los códigos en seis grupos: urbano, urbanizable, rústico común, protegido, agua y vías. Las proporciones de área de terreno usan los primeros cuatro grupos; las proporciones de lugares mantienen los polígonos de agua y vías en el denominador.
municipalities.landuse_classes.definition: The Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015 (PUT 2015, Junta de Planificación) gives each polygon a class code (CLASIPUT). The observatory gathers the codes into six groups: urban (SU, Suelo Urbano), urbanizable (SURP, Suelo Urbanizable Programado, and SURNP, Suelo Urbanizable No Programado), ordinary rural (SRC, Suelo Rústico Común), protected (SREP, Suelo Rústico Especialmente Protegido, and every SREP subtype), water (AGUA) and road (VIAL). The land-area shares (landuse_km2, urban_pct, urbanizable_pct, rustic_common_pct, protected_land_pct) use the first four groups only. The place shares (places_on_protected_land_pct, places_urban_pct) keep water and road polygons in the denominator. Every code and its meaning is in land.cls.
municipalities.landuse_classes.method: landuse.py upper-cases the CLASIPUT code, looks it up in a table (GROUPS) and, when the code is not in the table, tries the part before the first hyphen.
municipalities.landuse_classes.how_to_read: Urban, urbanizable and ordinary rural are the plan's general classes; the SREP codes add the reason for protection. Read the plan itself for what each class allows. In the 2015 plan, landuse.geojson holds 996 polygons; 68 of them carry the five less common subtypes (SREP-AE, SREP-AP, SREP-EA, SREP-EP, SREP-P).
caveats: Class meanings follow the plan's names; they are not legal advice and do not say what a given parcel may be used for.
The Plan's own version fields read PUT-2014 and 30-NOV-2015; this dictionary calls the version dated 30 November 2015 PUT 2015 (see land.put_layer).

The Junta de Planificación states no data license, and its site footer reads "Todos los derechos reservados". Check its terms before reusing the plan or figures computed from it. The Junta's page (read 2026-10-03) gives the plan a ten-year term and lists a review process for a new plan (PUT-2025). These classes describe the 2015 plan only.

land.put_layer.plain: The Junta de Planificación's land-use plan, shown as a map. It sorts all land in Puerto Rico into urban, urbanizable, ordinary rural and specially protected rural land, plus water and roads.
land.put_layer.plain_es: El plan de uso de terrenos de la Junta de Planificación, presentado como mapa. Clasifica todo el terreno de Puerto Rico en suelo urbano, urbanizable, rústico común y rústico especialmente protegido, además de agua y vías.
land.put_layer.definition: The file landuse.geojson holds 996 polygon features: 881 multi-part and 115 single polygons. They come from the Plan de Uso de Terrenos (PUT), the land-use plan of the Junta de Planificación de Puerto Rico. The version is dated 30 November 2015. The shapefile's own version fields read PUT-2014 and 30-NOV-2015; the observatory calls it the Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015. Each feature is one land class within one municipality, and a class can have several features in a municipality. Five attributes are kept: class code (cls), class name (label), group, display color and municipality (the field is named municipio).
land.put_layer.method: landuse.py (fetch_put) reads a copy of the Junta's official Plan shapefile (version of 30 November 2015) and reprojects it from the NAD83(2011) Puerto Rico State Plane projection to WGS 84. If that copy is missing, the build reads the public ArcGIS Online copy. Each polygon gets a label, group and color from the GROUPS table in landuse.py. The published file is a simplified display copy. Each place's land class is found on the full-detail polygons; area shares use the Plan layer's own Shape_Area attribute (see land.put_statistics).
land.put_layer.how_to_read: Use it for the broad pattern of where the Plan allows growth and where it protects land. The 2D map draws the four land groups and leaves water and road polygons out; they stay in the file.
caveats: The Plan dates from 30 November 2015. Land may since have been built on, reclassified or protected; the observatory does not track changes.
The Plan is a planning classification, not a zoning map. It does not say what may be built on a lot; see land.calificacion.
Polygons are simplified to about 110 m, so do not use the file to decide the class of a single lot.
On the 2D map the popup shows only the first land polygon at the click point.

This file is a simplified copy made by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) and reprojected to WGS 84. It is not the Junta de Planificación's official map; do not present it as such. The source states no data license (the Junta's site footer reserves all rights), so check the Junta's terms before reuse.

The Plan file splits some classes into several records within a municipality, by a type code (TIPO) in the Plan file that the observatory does not publish. Feature counts are not counts of zones or areas; use the area figures.

Legal basis: Art. 6.007 of the Código Municipal (Ley 107-2020) sets the three basic categories (urbano, urbanizable, rústico) for municipal territorial plans and says they must be consistent with the categories the Junta creates by regulation under Ley 550-2004, the law for the Plan de Uso de Terrenos. The state Plan uses the same category names. The summaries in this dictionary paraphrase the law and the Plan's class names; they are not legal definitions. The law cited is the law now in force; the law in force when the Plan was adopted may differ.

land.put_statistics.plain: Land-use shares for a municipality come from the Plan's own area figures, with water and roads left out. Each place listing in the places file gets the class of the Plan polygon that holds its pin; that test uses the full-detail polygons, not the published copy.
land.put_statistics.plain_es: Las proporciones de uso de terrenos de un municipio salen de las cifras de área del propio Plan, sin contar agua ni vías. Cada lugar del archivo de lugares recibe la clase del polígono del Plan que contiene su marcador; esa prueba usa los polígonos con todo su detalle, no la copia publicada.
land.put_statistics.definition: Area: for each municipality the build adds the Plan layer's Shape_Area (square meters, divided by 1,000,000) by group, leaving out water and road. Shares (urban_pct, urbanizable_pct, protected_land_pct, rustic_common_pct) divide each group's area by the sum of the four land groups. landuse_km2 holds the four group areas in km². Places: every listing in places.json gets land_use (class code) and land_group from the first Plan polygon that contains its pin, or none if no polygon does. The places_on_protected_land, places_on_protected_land_pct and places_urban_pct statistics in municipalities.json count listings by municipality and group.
land.put_statistics.method: build_landuse in landuse.py. Municipal areas are rounded to 0.1 km², so island-wide sums of them differ slightly from sums of the Plan's Shape_Area attribute. The percentage statistics divide by places inside any Plan polygon, including water and road polygons.
land.put_statistics.how_to_read: Use the shares for the municipality as a whole. Use the place statistics as a rough guide: they depend on where the pin is. In the Plan version of 30 November 2015, the island-wide totals of the municipal areas are 5,361 km² protected, 1,789 km² rustic, 1,190 km² urban and 68 km² urbanizable, 8,409 km² in all. Summing the Plan's Shape_Area attribute directly gives 5,361, 1,789, 1,191 and 69 km².
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the place-based statistics count all 32,541 listings, including places of worship and listings with confidence below 0.50. The other place statistics in the observatory use only the 24,209 places with confidence of 0.50 or more and no places of worship. The two bases give different results: in San Juan, 0.3% of all listings and 0.2% of the filtered places are on protected land.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 5,858 listings have their pin in a Vial (road) polygon and 172 in none, so the percentages are not shares of all places.

The Plan's Municipio field is matched by name. One water polygon is filed under the misspelling Guayanabo; it changes no figure, because water is left out of the area shares and places use their own pin location.

land.padus_acres.plain: The area of the protected area record in whole acres, as the US Geological Survey calculated it. In the 2026-10 snapshot the records run from under an acre to 387,847 acres.
land.padus_acres.plain_es: La superficie del registro del área protegida en acres enteros, según la calculó el USGS (Servicio Geológico de Estados Unidos). En el corte de datos de 2026-10, los registros van de menos de un acre a 387,847 acres.
land.padus_acres.definition: GIS_Acres is the area of the record's polygon (map shape) in acres, worked out in a geographic information system (GIS) and stored as a whole number. In the 2026-10 snapshot, values run from 0 to 387,847. The median is 5 acres. 90 records show 0. The largest is the Isla de Mona Natural Reserve, a marine protected area. One acre is 0.4047 hectares.
land.padus_acres.method: Copied from the Protected Areas Database of the United States (PAD-US). The build does not recompute it from the simplified display outlines.
land.padus_acres.how_to_read: Use it to compare the size of single records. Do not add the values up to get the total protected land.
caveats: Records overlap. A refuge can appear as a proclamation boundary, a wildlife refuge and a marine area, so a sum counts the same land more than once.
The 37 marine protected area records in the 2026-10 snapshot include open water, so their acres are not land area.
Some records are tiny. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 90 show 0 acres, and the median record is 5 acres.
The map popups print acres. The rest of the observatory uses square kilometres.

land.protected_place_flag.plain: A tourism place counts as inside a protected area when its map point falls in a polygon (map shape) of the Protected Areas Database of the United States (PAD-US) other than a proclamation outline. If it falls in several, the strictest Gap Analysis Project (GAP) status is kept.
land.protected_place_flag.plain_es: Un lugar turístico cuenta como dentro de un área protegida cuando su punto en el mapa cae en un polígono (figura del mapa) de PAD-US (base de datos de áreas protegidas de Estados Unidos) que no sea el contorno de una proclama. Si cae en varios, se conserva el estado GAP (Gap Analysis Project) más estricto.
land.protected_place_flag.definition: For every place the build tests its coordinates against the PAD-US polygons. Records with designation PROC (outlines) are skipped. If the point is in more than one other record, the record with the lowest GAP status wins. The place then carries that record's name (protected_area) and GAP status (protected_gap).
land.protected_place_flag.method: The build tests each place with the Shapely 'within' test against the unsimplified PAD-US polygons. Municipality counts (in_protected) use counted places only: confidence 0.50 or higher, places of worship excluded.
land.protected_place_flag.how_to_read: 'Inside a protected area' means the pin lies in a PAD-US record. It does not mean the place is in a nature reserve.
caveats: Snapshot 2026-10: 869 of 24,209 counted places (3.6%) are flagged. For 465 the record kept is a local park, for 13 military land and for 15 a historic or cultural area. 509 are in GAP 4 land.
In the same snapshot, one 'Unknown Local Park' record that spans the island holds 117 of the flagged places.
Only the pin is tested. The pin can be off the building.
If two records share the lowest GAP status, the build keeps one of them and no rule chooses which. The protected_area name can be either.

land.padus_manager.plain: A short code for the agency or group that manages the protected area. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 411 of the 665 records, all local parks, have no manager recorded.
land.padus_manager.plain_es: Un código corto para la agencia o el grupo que maneja el área protegida. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, 411 de los 665 registros, todos parques locales, no tienen administrador registrado.
land.padus_manager.definition: Mang_Name is the manager name code in the Protected Areas Database of the United States (PAD-US). In the 2026-10 snapshot, 13 codes occur. PAD-US describes the field as the land manager or administrative agency, standardised for the US. This file keeps the manager code only. It has no owner field.
land.padus_manager.how_to_read: Use the code to see which body to ask about a site. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 411 records have the code UNK. For those, look up the municipio instead.
caveats: PAD-US uses 'State' for the Puerto Rico government and its agencies.
The map popups print the raw code, for example 'managed by UNK', which means no manager is recorded.

land.padus_designation.plain: A short code for the type of protected area. Examples are local park (LP), state conservation area (SCA), marine protected area (MPA) and national wildlife refuge (NWR). The codes come from PAD-US, the Protected Areas Database of the United States, kept by the US Geological Survey.
land.padus_designation.plain_es: Un código corto para el tipo de área protegida. Algunos ejemplos son parque local (LP), área de conservación estatal (SCA), área marina protegida (MPA) y refugio nacional de vida silvestre (NWR). Los códigos vienen de PAD-US, la base de datos de áreas protegidas de Estados Unidos (Protected Areas Database of the United States), que mantiene el USGS (Servicio Geológico de Estados Unidos).
land.padus_designation.definition: Des_Tp is the designation type in PAD-US: the legal or planning category that created or recognises the area. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 22 codes occur in Puerto Rico. Local parks (LP) are 411 of the 665 records. The same place can appear under several types.
land.padus_designation.method: Copied from PAD-US without change. The map draws every record. Place flags skip records with code PROC.
land.padus_designation.how_to_read: The code says how an area is classed, not how well it is protected. Read GAP status for the level of protection and public access for entry.
caveats: The 2D map's popup spells out only some codes. It shows codes such as SCA, SRMA and MIL as raw letters. The list of values below gives the meaning of every code in the data.
PAD-US uses the word 'state' for the Puerto Rico government.
PAD-US counts military land, national cemeteries and local playgrounds as protected areas. Many of these are GAP status 4.

values.LP: Local Park: a park owned or run by a local government. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 411 records, all with manager UNK, public access OA and GAP status 4.
values.SCA: State Conservation Area: land the Puerto Rico government holds mainly to conserve nature. PAD-US calls any such government a 'state'. Many are named Reserva Natural. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 72 records.
values.PCON: Private Conservation: private land held for conservation. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 56 records, all managed by non-governmental organizations.
values.MPA: Marine Protected Area: sea area managed for conservation, such as natural reserves and the marine parts of national wildlife refuges. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 37 records.
values.SRMA: State Resource Management Area: state land managed for resources and several uses. Here mostly state forests (Bosque Estatal). In the 2026-10 snapshot: 19 records.
values.CONE: Conservation Easement: a legal agreement that limits development on land the owner keeps. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 13 records.
values.MIL: Military Land: bases, training areas and other land of the US Department of Defense. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 12 records, all closed to the public in PAD-US.
values.NWR: National Wildlife Refuge: refuge land managed by the US Fish and Wildlife Service. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 10 records.
values.PROC: Approved or Proclamation Boundary: the outer boundary approved for a park, forest, refuge or historic site. It outlines an area and is not separate protected land. The map draws these outlines. Place flags ignore them. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 7 records.
values.WSR: Wild and Scenic River: a river segment in the national Wild and Scenic Rivers system. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 6 records, all managed by the US Forest Service.
values.SOTH: State Other or Unknown: state-level land whose type is not given. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 5 records.
values.HCA: Historic or Cultural Area: a federal historic or cultural site, such as a national historic site or a national cemetery. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 3 records.
values.SP: State Park: a park run by the Puerto Rico government. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 2 records.
values.REA: Research or Educational Area: land used for research or teaching, such as an experimental forest or an agricultural experiment station. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 2 records.
values.POTH: Private Other or Unknown: private land with another or unknown purpose. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 2 records.
values.IRA: Inventoried Roadless Area: national forest land that the Forest Service has inventoried as roadless. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 2 records.
values.NF: National Forest: El Yunque National Forest. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1 record.
values.LRMA: Local Resource Management Area: local-government land managed for resources. Here a community forest. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1 record.
values.PFOR: Private Forest Stewardship: private forest land under a stewardship program. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1 record.
values.SHCA: State Historic or Cultural Area: a state historic or cultural site. Here an Indigenous ceremonial park. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1 record.
values.RNA: Research Natural Area: land kept natural for research. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1 record.
values.WA: Wilderness Area: federal wilderness. Here El Toro Wilderness. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1 record.

land.padus_unit_name.plain: The name of the protected area record, as the US Geological Survey lists it. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 665 records share 640 different names.
land.padus_unit_name.plain_es: El nombre del registro del área protegida, tal como lo presenta el USGS (Servicio Geológico de Estados Unidos). En el corte de datos de 2026-10, 665 registros comparten 640 nombres distintos.
land.padus_unit_name.definition: Unit_Nm is the unit name in the Protected Areas Database of the United States (PAD-US). Each polygon (map shape) is one record. A named place can have several records. In the 2026-10 snapshot, for example, five records are named Culebra National Wildlife Refuge: a proclamation boundary, a marine protected area, two national wildlife refuge records (Gap Analysis Project (GAP) status 1 and 2) and a conservation easement. Names are in Spanish, English or both.
land.padus_unit_name.method: The build downloads the PAD-US records for Puerto Rico and keeps Unit_Nm unchanged.
land.padus_unit_name.how_to_read: Use the name to find the area. For a count of areas, count distinct names with care, because one name can have several records.
caveats: Some local-park records have generic names, for example a facility type rather than a park name.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, one record named 'Unknown Local Park' is a single record made of many separate small parcels (a MultiPolygon) spread across the island, 1,126 acres in all. It is not one park.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, at least one name says '(proposed)' (Reserva Natural Torrecilla Alta), so a record can describe a proposed area, not yet protected land.

land.protected_layer.plain: A map layer of the US Geological Survey's protected-areas database, from El Yunque National Forest to local parks (665 records in the 2026-10 snapshot). Records overlap, so the number of records is not a count of separate areas, and 'protected' here includes recreation and military land.
land.protected_layer.plain_es: Una capa del mapa con la base de datos de áreas protegidas del USGS (Servicio Geológico de Estados Unidos), desde el Bosque Nacional El Yunque hasta parques locales (665 registros en el corte de datos de 2026-10). Los registros se superponen, así que el número de registros no es un conteo de áreas separadas, y aquí "protegida" incluye terrenos recreativos y militares.
land.protected_layer.definition: The 'Protected areas' layer draws every record of the Protected Areas Database of the United States (PAD-US) in protected.geojson in green, including the proclamation outlines. Clicking a point opens a popup with the name, designation, manager, public access, acres and Gap Analysis Project (GAP) status for up to two records under the click, the same in the 2D map and the 3D view.
land.protected_layer.method: protected.geojson holds the PAD-US outlines simplified to about 5 m (0.00005 degrees). The 2D layer is green at 30% opacity, and the 3D layer at 35%. No record is hidden.
land.protected_layer.how_to_read: Overlapping outlines are stacked, so a darker patch can be several records. Check the designation and GAP status before reading a patch as nature reserve.
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot the layer includes military land, national cemeteries and 411 local parks.
Outlines are simplified for display. Place flags use the unsimplified outlines.
The route planner in the 2D map and the 3D view counts every protected polygon, including the proclamation outlines. The place flag skips them.

PAD-US combines data from federal, state and local agencies and nonprofit partners, so the quality and age of boundaries vary. USGS advises asking the managing agency directly for authoritative boundaries.
PAD-US protected areas are not the land-use plan's 'Suelo Rústico Especialmente Protegido' class. The two come from different sources and draw different boundaries.

land.padus_gap_status.plain: A code from 1 to 4 that shows how strongly an area is managed to protect nature. Codes 1 and 2 are managed for biodiversity. Code 3 may allow uses such as mining or logging. Code 4 has no known requirement to protect biodiversity.
land.padus_gap_status.plain_es: Un código de 1 a 4 que indica cuán estrictamente se maneja un área para proteger la naturaleza. Los códigos 1 y 2 se manejan para la biodiversidad. El código 3 puede permitir usos como la minería o la tala. El código 4 no tiene ningún requisito conocido de proteger la biodiversidad.
land.padus_gap_status.definition: GAP_Sts is the status code of the Gap Analysis Project (GAP) of the US Geological Survey, as carried in the Protected Areas Database of the United States (PAD-US). It sorts areas by how they are managed for biodiversity. In the 2026-10 snapshot the counts are: code 4, 440; code 2, 181; code 1, 25; code 3, 19. The values are text digits.
land.padus_gap_status.method: Copied from PAD-US without change. When a place sits in several protected areas, the build keeps the one with the strictest (lowest) GAP status.
land.padus_gap_status.how_to_read: 1 is the strictest and 4 the loosest. A high count of places in GAP 4 land says little about nature protection.
caveats: The status describes how land is managed on paper. It does not measure habitat condition.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 59% of the counted places flagged as in a protected area are in GAP 4 land (509 of 869).

PAD-US words code 1 as managed for biodiversity with natural disturbance allowed. Do not read it as a strict nature reserve. The 2D map popup words the codes differently: strict nature reserve (1), managed for biodiversity (2), multiple use, some extraction (3) and no known biodiversity mandate (4). Those are the map's labels, not PAD-US wording.

values.1: Managed for biodiversity. Natural disturbance, such as fire or flooding, is allowed to happen or is imitated by management. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 25 records.
values.2: Managed for biodiversity, but natural disturbance is suppressed, for example fires are put out. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 181 records.
values.3: Managed for multiple uses. Extractive uses such as mining or logging, or off-highway vehicle use, may be allowed. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 19 records.
values.4: No known requirement to protect biodiversity. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 440 records, including all 411 local parks.

exposure.pop_protected.plain: How many residents are inside the outline of a protected area such as a park, forest or reserve, counted for each municipio, barrio and census tract.
exposure.pop_protected.plain_es: Cuántas personas residentes hay dentro del contorno de un área protegida, como un parque, un bosque o una reserva, en cada municipio, barrio y sector censal.
exposure.pop_protected.definition: Two fields hold the count for each area. protected: the residents of every census block whose internal point lies inside a USGS PAD-US protected area, other than a proclamation boundary (which outlines whole islands or refuges and is not managed land). protected_strict: the same inside areas with GAP status 1 or 2 (a strict nature reserve, or land managed for biodiversity). Both read site/data/protected.geojson. For the whole island, 58,220 residents (1.8%) are inside a protected area and 30,716 (0.9%) inside a strictly protected one.
exposure.pop_protected.method: exposure.py counts each 2020 Census block whole, by its internal point (the Census Bureau's point that always lies inside the block): inside the polygons of a layer, or within 400 m of a stop. It adds the block's 2020 residents up to the municipio, the barrio and the census tract that hold it, so the three files agree and counts add up exactly between levels. It writes nothing unless every area's total equals the crosswalk's and every set lies inside its superset (the area flooded at 2 ft is inside the area flooded at 3 ft; a stop with a current timetable is a stop).
exposure.pop_protected.how_to_read: Compare areas by share: divide a count by the area's total (the total field), which puts a small barrio and a large municipio on one scale. To get a share for a group of areas (the island, a region), add the counts and the totals first, then divide; do not average the shares. It shows where homes lie within the outline of conserved land, which matters for planning, not how many people live on managed public land.
caveats: PAD-US includes parks, forests, refuges, local recreation areas and conservation lands, so an urban park counts. An outline can also include private land inside the boundary of a reserve.
A census block is counted whole by one point, so a block that a boundary cuts is counted in or out by its internal point: near an edge the count can be higher or lower than the true number.
exposure.pop_protected.geography: 78 municipios, 901 barrios and 981 census tracts, in three files

land.soil_chemistry.plain: The acidity, organic matter, salinity and lime of the top 30 cm of the soil.
land.soil_chemistry.plain_es: La acidez, la materia orgánica, la salinidad y la cal de los primeros 30 cm del suelo.
land.soil_chemistry.definition: Thickness-weighted means over the horizons of the main soil in the top 30 cm: ph is the pH in water (1:1, ph1to1h2o_r), om the organic matter in percent of weight (om_r), ec the electrical conductivity in decisiemens per metre, a measure of salinity (ec_r), and caco3 the calcium carbonate equivalent in percent, the lime (caco3_r). Empty for land types with no soil.
land.soil_chemistry.method: soils.py reads the representative values of every horizon of the main soil (chorizon) and weights each by the part of its thickness that lies in the top 30 cm.
land.soil_chemistry.how_to_read: pH under 5.5 is strongly acid and over 8.4 strongly alkaline; organic matter over 8% is an organic soil; salinity over 4 dS/m harms most crops; lime is grouped as none (under 0.5%), little (0.5-5%), moderate (5-15%) and very high (over 15%).
caveats: These are NRCS's representative values for the soil series, not measurements at the place.
Planning scale: the value belongs to the typical soil of the map unit, not to a single lot; it does not replace a study of the site.

land.soil_farm.method: soils.py maps the farmlndcl text to the four classes with its FARM table.

caveats: Planning scale: the value belongs to the typical soil of the map unit, not to a single lot; it does not replace a study of the site.

land.soil_cover.how_to_read: Where cover is Urban land, the soil described is the one under and between the buildings.
